'''Malcolm John Williamson''' (2 November 1950 – 15 September 2015) was a British mathematician and cryptographer. In 1974 he developed what is now known as [[Diffie–Hellman key exchange]].<ref name=singh>{{Cite book |first=Simon |last=Singh |author-link=Simon Singh |title=[[The Code Book]] |publisher=Doubleday |year=1999 |pages=279–292 }}</ref> He was then working at [[Government Communications Headquarters|GCHQ]] and was therefore unable to publicise his research as his work was classified. [[Martin Hellman]], who independently developed the key exchange at the same time, received credit for the discovery until Williamson's research was declassified by the British government in 1997.<ref name=singh/>

Williamson studied at [[Manchester Grammar School]], winning first prize in the 1968 [[British Mathematical Olympiad]].<ref>A.Gardiner "The Mathematical Olympiad Handbook" Oxford University Press, 1997</ref> He also won a Silver prize<ref>{{Citation  | title = The Science Teacher volume 11 number 1 (October 1967) pages 30 and 31  | year = 1967  | url = http://www.imo-register.org.uk/1967-report-st.html| access-date = 26 Jan 2009}}</ref> at the 1967 [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] in Cetinje, Yugoslavia and a Gold prize<ref>{{Citation  | title = New Science Teacher volume 12 number 2 (December 1968) pages 31–35  | year = 1968  | url = http://www.imo-register.org.uk/1968-report-st.html| access-date = 26 Jan 2009}}</ref> at the 1968 International Mathematical Olympiad in [[Moscow]].<ref>{{IMO results|id=10018}}</ref>  He read mathematics at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], graduating in 1971. After a year at [[Liverpool University]], he joined [[GCHQ]], and worked there until 1982.

From 1985 to 1989 Williamson worked at Nicolet Instruments in Madison, Wisconsin where he was the primary author on two digital hearing aid patents.<ref>US Patent 5091952 - Feedback suppression in digital signal processing hearing aids</ref><ref>US Patent 5027410 - Adaptive, programmable signal processing and filtering for hearing aids</ref>  After that, he moved to the [[Institute for Defense Analyses#Center for Communications and Computing|IDA Center for Communications Research, La Jolla]],<ref>{{Citation | title = Scale-free and power law distributions via fixed points and convergence of (thinning and conditioning) transformations | journal = Electronic Communications in Probability | volume = 19 | year = 2014 | number = 39 | pages = 1–10 | doi = 10.1214/ECP.v19-2923| last1 = Arratia | first1 = Richard |author-link=Richard Arratia | last2 = Liggett | first2 = Thomas | last3 = Williamson | first3 = Malcolm | s2cid = 15038587 | arxiv = 1306.3017 }}</ref> where he worked for the rest of his career.

His contributions to the invention of [[public-key cryptography]], together with [[Clifford Cocks]] and [[James H. Ellis|James Ellis]], have been recognized by the IEEE Milestone Award #104<ref>{{Citation | title = Milestones:Invention of Public-key Cryptography, 1969 - 1975 | year = 2010 | url = https://ethw.org/Milestones:Invention_of_Public-key_Cryptography,_1969_-_1975 | access-date = 4 Feb 2022}}</ref> in 2010 and by induction into the [[NSA Hall of Honor|Cryptologic Hall of Honor]] in 2021.
